utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And approximately what percentage of the total data on missing persons gathered during the course of this action was gathered on the basis of the standardised missing persons questionnaire that you participated in the design of?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Over 99 per cent. It would probably be justified to say that only in exceptional cases information was collected by way of a shortened version of the questionnaire, and this was primarily in the case of those families which requested postmortem remains. Not missing persons but the postmortem remains thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In section 11 of your report at page 16 of the English and 6 of the B/C/S, you describe three things that were done with the data after they were collected. First a determination was made as to whether a given disappearance occurred in connection with war time events. Second, if multiple questionnaires had been filled out with respect to a single person, the data was merged. And finally, the data was put into a computer database. Did you take part in any of these three steps?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I took part in both of the stages. I -- in both of the steps you just described. In the first step which was reading every personal file in order to confirm whether the disappearance was within the purview of the then state commission or rather whether the disappearance, which was reported, had anything to do with war events. I also participated in step two, which was the merging of all the files in those cases when the requests for the search of one in the same person had been filed by different people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And who then put the data into the database?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The database is an electronic database which was previously prepared, and when it comes to the entry of data, we engaged a previously trained personnel, those people who had been trained about the data entry into the electronic database.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And approximately when was the data put into the database?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The data was put into the database immediately after all the checks were completed, the checks that we have just described. It probably took a month or so to perform all the checks and then another month for all the collected data to be put into the database. In other words, I believe that before the beginning of May 1994, all the data was put into the electronic database.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And after the data was entered into the electronic database, what was done with the paper files?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The paper files were coded for an easier manipulation, and they were archived so as to make them available and accessible to the every-day work of the personnel of the administration for missing and detained persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. I'd now like to turn to sections 24 to 29 of your report, which deal with identifications. This is pages 25 to 30 of the English and pages 10 to 12 of the B/C/S. You describe the process of identification of exhumed remains. Can you briefly describe the role of your administration in co-ordinating the identification of exhumed remains?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way very briefly. One could say that the administration for missing and detained persons was in charge of the following parts of the job which is also described by the government decree. Primarily, the administration for missing and detained persons collected information about all the exhumed victims with a view to their identification which included anti-mortem information, postmortem information, operative information about the possible identity of exhumed victims and includes the DNA analysis as well. That would be the first step when it comes to the collection of information about the exhumed victims and their identification. The second task of the administration for detained and missing persons was to organise and co-ordinate the processes, to identify the exhumed postmortem remains. After that what follow is the collection of data about the identified victims and maintaining records about identified victims, as well as the collection and merging of all of the documentation covering all the identified victims. That would be, in short, all the tasks of the administration of missing and detained persons within the process of identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Are staff from your administration present when remains are identified?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. The assistant minister who was the head of the administration for missing and detained persons, Colonel Ivan Grujic, was present during every identification process.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And if remains are positively identified, how was your administration officially informed of that fact?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The administration was provided with the findings. However, I would like to say that one of the jobs and the competencies of the administration was establish the premortem identity. Also, the administration maintained records of all unidentified persons that would from time to time be publicly disclosed in those places where there was the largest number of victims, and in addition to that, as I've already said, the administration was also provided with DNA findings confirming the match between the benchmark findings such as blood of the next of kin and the postmortem remains. And based on that information, the administration established a list of persons for identification and the system that was in place was used to inform the families about identification. The system functions in the following way: The families of the civilians whose identification was pending was directly informed and then they informed the Red Cross about the time and the place of identification. Croatian veterans also informed, or rather, the Croatian veterans were informed by the relevant offices in charge of the veterans as well as the Red Cross. In other words, the families received direct information about the upcoming identification and they were invited to attend the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And it's at those identifications that the preliminary identification becomes a final identification; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: If the family confirmed the result of the identification, then, yes. In any case, the family had a final say in confirming or denying to confirm the identification results.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And what does your administration do with the records of a missing person whose remains have been exhumed and identified?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: In that case, we entered information about the date and the time of the identification of postmortem remains in the electronic base. The paper file would be complemented by the records of the identified patient, dental records, the DNA analysis as well as the report of the institution that carried out the postmortem analysis, and that file was then transferred from the archives of missing persons into the archives of identified persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In section 10 of your report, page 15 English and page 6 B/C/S, you describe a second action carried out by your administration between 2002 and 2006 to gather data on persons who went missing following Operation Flash and Operation Storm. Can you just briefly describe how your administration initiated this action?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, the first action to collect information about missing persons, as we already stated, was carried out in 1994. In operations flash and storm which took place after the first action to collect data, they were in 1995, a certain number of the citizens of the Republic of Croatia went missing. An initiative was launched by the then commission of the Republic of Croatia for detained persons to collect -- to start collecting information about people who went missing during operations flash and storm. Bearing in mind the fact that most of the families of the missing persons who went missing in operations flash and storm resided in the territory of the Republic of Serbia and some of them in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the action to collect data was preceded by an agreement with the official bodies of the Republic of Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina who were also involved in the search for missing persons as well as an agreement with the international committee of the Red Cross which co-operated in the direct collection of information about missing persons. Also, what preceded the collection of data was training of the Red Cross personnel as well as the training of the Red Cross of Serbia and the Red Cross of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Their officials also were involved in the collection of data. It should be emphasised here that the data collected were collected based on the same criteria and the same methodology as was the case in the collection of data about the missing persons in the action that was carried out in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you've described two actions for us. One in 1994 and one from 2002 to 2006 in which your administration gathered data. Now, in section 30 of your report, pages 30 to 32 of English, and pages 13 and 14 of the B/C/S, you summarised the data on the missing persons collected during these two actions. What was the ethnicity of the majority of the victims for whom you collected data in the first action, that is the action conducted in 1994?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Most were Croatians. I believe that this can be seen from other document that I enclosed. 87 per cent of the missing persons were Croatians. In the second action to collect data between 2004 and 2006 which continued even thereafter, most of the people who went missing were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In this first group that was predominantly Croat, you said that there are 176 [sic] persons who were still missing of whom 542 are civilians. Of those 542 missing civilians, how many are Croats?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, could you please bear with me. Out of 1076 missing persons, according to the records on the date of the report, which was in 2008, 542 persons were civilians, and of that number 461 persons were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you. In section 31 of your report, you mention two groups of persons whose remains have been exhumed and identified. Section 31 describes the first group as having been exhumed from "mass and individual graves" while the second group was exhumed from "common graves following the humane 'asanacija' or terrain restoration of mortal remains from the storm military police action." My question is, can you briefly describe the difference between a mass grave as you use the term in your report, and a common grave created as a result of "asanacija?"

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: There is no common accepted term for -- definition of the term mass grave. Croatia has adopted the recommendations of UN experts involved in arbitration according to whom mass grave is a place where the remains of three or more persons were buried illegally without any markings and any show of respect towards the mortal remains. This would be a mass grave. As far as a common grave is concerned, which were the result of the exhumation, postmortem remains buried in common graves were buried in keeping with the Geneva Conventions. There is a relevant and required distance between mortal remains. The place where they were buried is duty marked. Those would be the main differences. There is also documentation about the postmortem remains buried in common graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Still in section 31 of your report, pages 33 to 34 of the English and 14 and 15 of the B/C/S, you give the statistics for these two groups, that is, the group exhumed from mass and individual graves versus the group exhumed from common graves following the "asanacija." My question is, what was the ethnicity of the majority of the people exhumed from the mass and individual graves as defined in your report as opposed to the people exhumed from the common graves created after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: In the first case those were Croats predominantly. 87 per cent of the exhumed and identified victims from mass and individual graves were Croats. As far as the persons exhumed from common graves is concerned, in 90 per cent of the cases approximately they were of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And of this first predominantly Croat group, you indicated that 3.100 people had been identified and that of those 3.100 identified persons, 1.881 were civilians. My question is, can you tell me of those 1.881 identified civilians how many were Croats?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Out of 1.881 persons, according to the information provided by the families of those identified persons, 1.488 were of Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you a little bit about the information contained in the charts of victims of various incidents charged in the indictment in this case. These charts are in your report at ERN pages 0641-2240 to 0641-2251 of the B/C/S and pages 89 through 107 of the English. My first question is, were these charts based on the computer database or the paper records maintained by your administration or both?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The data in the electronic database are identical with the data contained in the paper files. However, the tables are based on both, both the electronic database and the paper files.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you about the meaning of some of the abbreviations used in these charts. There is a legend to these abbreviations at ERN page 0641-2252 of the B/C/S which is pages 108 to 109 of the English, but I'd like to ask you a few more questions to clarify exactly what they mean. Starting with the first abbreviation "NES" which indicates a missing person. What does it mean when the person has the designation "in ES" beside their name?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: I must admit that there is no EES, there's only NES which means that the person is indeed missing. That the request has been filed to search for that person but that that person's lot is still uncertain, that it still hasn't been established what has happened to the person. NES, missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you. And does your administration have a missing persons questionnaire on record for everyone who has the abbreviation NES by their name in your report?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: The next category is "ID" or identified person. What does that abbreviation beside a persons name indicate?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: That abbreviation indicates that the mortal remains of a person have been positively identified and accepted by the family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Does your administration have an identification report for every person who has the abbreviation "ID" beside his or her name in your report?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: The next category is POG, or person killed, according to the records of 12.078 killed during the aggression on the Republic of Croatia. What does this category mean?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: It means that the person is in the records of persons killed during the war in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Does your administration maintain official records regarding this category?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The administration for detained and missing persons does not have within its purview maintaining records about killed persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And what bodies of the Croatian government are responsible for maintaining this information?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The bodies in Croatia who are charged with keeping records on killed persons are the Ministry of Health and Social Welfare who maintain records on killed civilians as well as the Ministry of the Family Affairs Veterans --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please stop and repeat from the second sentence on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, I believe that the interpreters lost track of your answer. You had just said that the Ministry of the Family and Veterans is involved in keeping records on killed -- no, you had said that the Ministry of Health maintains the records of the killed civilians, and you were getting ready to say what the role of some part of the Ministry of Family Affairs and Veterans Affairs was. Could you tell us what the role of the Ministry of Family Affairs and Veterans Affairs is in keeping the records of the killed persons?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Health is tasked with keeping records on killed civilians. Whereas the Ministry of Family Affairs, Veterans and Intergenerational Solidarity, however not the administration for detained and missing persons in which I work, but rather the administration who takes care of Croatian war veterans altogether is tasked with maintaining records on killed Croatian defence forces members.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And where did you get the information regarding the people that you list with this status POG in your report?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Above all I had access to the register of killed persons in connection with war time activities in Croatia, but there was also information that was used in previous testimonies by the assistant minister in charge of detained and missing persons namely Lieutenant-Colonel Ivan Grujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: The next category is ZPO, which according to the English translation means search for mortal remains, request submitted by their family to the administration for detainees and missing persons. What does this category mean?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: In keeping with the methodology of the ICRC, the administration for missing and detained persons also collected information about persons who were killed and who can be found in the registers of killed persons. But their families do not know where their mortal remains have been buried. This category differs from the category of missing persons in this respect because when it comes to missing persons, their family members have no information about them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Does your administration have a request for search for mortal remains on file with respect to every victim in the category ZPO in your report?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. The administration for detained and missing persons has all requests for search for mortal remains. I believe at this moment there's a total of 420 such requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And finally, the category RSL, what does that abbreviation mean?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: It means that the case is solved. It's about a person which was considered missing; however, its fate has been established, not through the process of identification of mortal remains though because the group of identified persons is a separate group and marked differently. These are persons whose fate has been resolved differently. Their mortal remains may have been found in the places where they had residence or possibly those are people who died natural death and their remains were found subsequently, or they may have been persons whose family reported them as missing but it was later on established that they were, in fact, alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I tender this witness's expert report, which has been uploaded in e-court as 65 ter number 5335.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P514, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P514 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could we now please have 65 ter number 5337.1 on the screen. This is the second proofing note for this witness dated 26 May 2010, which has been initialled and signed by this witness. The proofing note contains the text of two e-mails send by Ms. Bilic updating and correcting certain matters in her report, and if there's no objection I would tender it as a Prosecution exhibit at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, may I just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P515, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P515 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, in your e-mail of 21 May 2010, which is included in the proofing note just admitted, you stated: "I'm informing you that the information on the missing exhumed and identified persons has slightly changed. However, these changes are not so significant to change the age, generic status, and ethnic structure." Could you please briefly explain what these changes were and why they did not have any significant impact on the items you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: While preparing the report, and I'm referring to information from July 2008, the administration for detained and missing persons had 1.076 persons registered. I mean, the persons from the first cycle of collecting information back in 2004. From July 2008 until now, a certain number of missing persons has been resolved so that now they total 1.049. These cases which have been resolved in the meantime are not so numerous though as to affect the gender structure, the ethnic makeup, or the age makeup, or the status makeup as shown in the PowerPoint presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And did you say how many persons cases had been resolved of those 1.076?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. 47 cases have been resolved to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So do I understand you correctly that essentially those 47 cases out of 1.076 don't have an influence on the statistical breakdown listed in your report?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: During the course of your preparation for your testimony here today, did you review a significant number of missing person questionnaires here in the Prosecution's offices?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did you recognise the format of those questionnaires?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised it. They are original documents of the administration for detained and missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, is this the same form that you helped design and that you've worked with during your 16 years in the state administrations for detainees and missing persons?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the format of questionnaire used by the department for detained and missing persons to collect information about these persons and it uses this format in its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And did you make comments regarding the authenticity of these missing persons questionnaires?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: I established that the questionnaires are credible.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And by credible, do you mean authentic?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did you also make comments regarding what those documents showed about the time and place of disappearance of certain people?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I put forward information such as the date and place where they went missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Were your comments then put into a chart and were those charts then read back to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, the data was inserted into of the table. The contents of the table were read out to me, and it corresponded to what I had stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And did you then sign the charts on which these comments had been recorded?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I signed the charts.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter number 5333 on the screen. This is the chart listing the documents reviewed by Ms. Bilic showing her comments regarding the authenticity. I have copies of these charts for the Chamber and Defence. I didn't have a chance to hand them out before, but I have them if they are necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam usher, could you collect the available documentation and distribute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, do you recognise this chart on the screen before you as the chart upon which you recorded your observations regarding the various documents you reviewed here in the Prosecution's offices?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: I recognised it. It is the very table, the chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And do you recognise your signature?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I tender this chart as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Objection on the same basis as the previous chart. We were given it at 1.00 today. We haven't had a chance to look at it. We don't know what it contains and its significance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: If the position is the same as it is with respect to the other chart, that the Defence have the night to review it and then that the decision be made tomorrow, that's acceptable to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Irrespective of what the decision would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Well, we accept --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are so generous.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I would just mention, Your Honour, that there are no new documents in this chart, just for the sake of clarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we had two items, as I said before, the one is the new entries that apparently doesn't play a role here and the other is the possibility to verify whether the data on this chart are -- do correspond with the information, the underlying documentation. I suggest that we take the same approach. Madam Registrar, the number for this document to be marked for identification would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P516 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And will keep that status for the time being. Mr. Farr, I'm looking at the clock. It's time for a break, I would say, and then I take it in view of your earlier estimate that you easily conclude the examination-in-chief by 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, I was intending to tender the underlying exhibits to this chart as well. I think it's a different situation. The Defence has had these for a long period of time. This part isn't a surprise. I don't know with whether the Chamber would prefer to address that now or after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends what else you have for after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I do still have a few matters, probably 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we first have a break and we resume at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for the late time we resume. Mr. Farr, you were about to tender the underlying documents, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And there are 81 documents that Ms. Bilic has authenticated, they were all noticed to be used with this witness. Her comment on authenticity was simply that they were authentic, this is a form that she helped to develop, that she's worked with for 16 year. I understand that, you know, the Defence may wish to cross-examine her on comments that she's made about the documents, but as to the admission of the documents, I think that would be appropriate at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are speculating on what the Defence apparently would wish or not wish to do. Any objections? Here at least we are rid of the new documents because these are were all disclosed in time, if I understood you well, and it's different from the previous series.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. The only -- I think Mr. Farr is almost right. The only caveat I would add is that we don't know what the witness's comments, the significance of the witness's comments in relation to the exhibits. They may relate to the admissibility issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that. At the same time if we would not have a chart with her comments, they could have been tendered as disclosed timely and relevant in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, it seems to be more a matter of when your cross-examination starts, than whether it affects the admissibility. But we leave it open. I mean, it's well understood that if the comments would cast any totally different light on the admission of the others, of course, we'll revisit that matter and then -- but the 81 documents, as such, there's no of this moment -- at this moment no objection to admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, same position, different position?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic. That's a good answer to my question, same or different, then to say yes, Mr. Petrovic, that really helps me out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, I misspoke. We have nothing to add to what Mr. Jordash has already said so we have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the numbers for the 81 documents would be, or would you prefer to prepare a chart first? These 81 documents are admitted into evidence, numbers to be assigned by Madam Registrar and she will put them on the list. Mr. Farr, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I would just note that there are some situations where our victim lists indicate a number of possible spellings for particular names. These missing persons questionnaires do provide more specific detail on that point, and I've also would know that where Ms. Bilic's report lists a given individual as being missing or unidentified but we do not have the corresponding missing persons questionnaire or identification report, we've noted that in her authentication chart, and as she has indicated, her administration does have all of those underlying documents that can be requested from her administration, should that become necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Her comments are based upon what is available in your databases, rather than what may be elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Her comments on her authentication chart are based on physical documents that we have that were shown to her. The matters in her report are based on her significantly more complete archive in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It was not without reason that I use the word "comments" because that's one of the columns, I think you earlier referred to that as the column in which comments were made. Yes, that's clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, before the break you confirmed that your administration has a missing persons questionnaire for each person listed as missing in your report. You also confirmed that your administration has an identification report for each person listed as identified in your report. I just have one follow-up on that. Does your administration also have the missing person's questionnaire for people who were later identified and who therefore now have the designation ID?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, for some of them. I must say that some of the identified persons from the missing persons category are from the missing persons category but others are not. The persons who were previously registered as missing and whose mortal remains were subsequently identified, are persons for whom our administration has questionnaires who were filled out -- that were filled out in 1994 during the -- our appeal to renew the search requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to ask you briefly about the victims from Skabrnja listed in your report. All of the victims from Skabrnja that we have now in our indictment are listed as killed in your report. My question is, did any of these persons ever have the status of missing persons?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: No, no person on the list of victims from Skabrnja was ever on the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The list of missing persons was established in early 1994. The victims from Skabrnja on this list are persons whose mortal remains were delivered to the Croatian authorities in November 1991, as far as I know, after which the procedure for identifying and burying them was carried out. There was no need, therefore, and no justification for these persons to be on the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you a couple of -- questions about a couple of the exhumations you attended. Were you present at the exhumation carried out at the Bacin Skela or Bacin ferry location?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was present at the exhumation at Bacin Skela.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And approximately how long did that exhumation last?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The exhumation was carried out in March 1997, and it went on for about ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Were you present for that whole ten-day period?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was present throughout the exhumation at Bacin.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd now like to play two short clips from 65 ter 2589, which is the video with ERN V000-5117. The first clip runs from 3 minutes and 12 seconds to 5 minutes and 40 seconds. The transcript has been marked as "clip 1" and I believe it has been provided to the booths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, you may have noticed that on a video-clip played previously today, that the Chamber wondered what it learned from it. I hope it's not a similar exercise, hard music, a lot of atmosphere but no real information which assists the Chamber in making the determinations it will have to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I don't think that will be the case. Although, I have to say the music is similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm also, Mr. Groome, from what I understand you are more or less the senior in the team. I don't know whether it was clear what I said earlier today, and we'd like to keep it as clean as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have not seen the video-clip before, but I have discussed it about Mr. Farr, and I do trust his judgement on it. Mr. Farr being aware of the admonition of the Court, says that it not similar to that earlier video-clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not only that it should not be similar, but it should bring us something in addition to what the evidence has brought us until that moment apart from -- I'm not saying that the Chamber is not blind for emotion and for, but the Chamber is -- well, Mr. Farr, I think the message has been clear enough. You have discussed it with Mr. Groome. Let's for the -- you have two video-clips, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you want, we can look at -- I'll review the tapes tonight and the witness is coming back tomorrow and I can personally attest to why I believe it's directly relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think I sent a clear message. Mr. Farr has discussed the message with you, you trust that Mr. Farr has -- his judgement is professional. Let's see whether that's the case and look at the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I'll just first ask the witness this question:

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: During the course of your preparation for testimony here today, did you have the opportunity to review several video-clips with me?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you recall what those video-clips depicted?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Chamber what those video-clips depicted?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The video-clips depicted how the micro location of the mass grave at Bacin Skela was found, and then the exhumation of the mortal remains is shown as well as the interviews with the participants in the exhumation process.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll defer to the Chamber's judgement as to whether that's the kind of evidence that might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am addressing you, Mr. Jordash and Mr. Bakrac. Is there any challenge as to whether the right place was found, the way in which people were led to that place, whether the exhumation causes any concerns as far as you are concerned? Is there anything in the videos which you may be familiar with which touches upon an issue in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under those circumstances you want to show us something where there's apparently no issue in dispute. If you would disagree or if you would take a minute to discuss it with Mr. Groome, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, did you also attend the exhumation carried out at a well in Daljski Atar?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did attend the exhumation at the well at Daljski Atar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And approximately how long did that exhumation last?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Approximately a week, and it was done in October 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Based on your attendance at that exhumation, can you tell us what was found?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: In the mass grave at Daljski Atar, we found the mortal remains of 23 persons. So far the mortal remains of 20 persons have been positively identified. The process of identification has shown that the persons who were found in that mass grave in the well were locals from Erdut who were taken away from their homes on several occasions in 1991 and in early 1992. Depending on the time they were taken away, or rather, the position of the bodies was in direct correlation with the time they were taken away. Those who were taken away first were at the bottom of the well, whereas, those who are taken away last in early 1992, their bodies were at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps one question. You may have noticed that the Chamber is inclined to rely on reports. Now, is there anything in the two exhumations which is extraordinary, which is different from what is usually found or what is not reflected in the reports we receive on exhumation and identification of bodies? Is there anything special, or is it -- would it give any information which we would not have by carefully reading the report and.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there's nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Farr, if there's any need to show the videos in re-examination based on what the cross-examination may reveal, then, of course, the Chamber will consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Farr. We have discussed with the parties when your cross-examination would start and in order to be better prepared both Defence teams have asked us to allow them to start tomorrow. The same is true, by the way, for another witness who testified today. Therefore, we'd like to see you back tomorrow in the afternoon and then how we are going to organise that exactly is not entirely clear to me yet because we have received estimates for the totality of the cross-examination, so whether you would have to wait for awhile, whether you would be the first one or whether it would be Mr. Strinovic, which I take it that you are aware that he was a witness today as well, is still uncertain, but there's -- I hardly can imagine that we would not within the first two hours of tomorrow's afternoon session that we could conclude your testimony, to hear your testimony. Therefore, you will be excused for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow at quarter past 2.00. And I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone, that would include other witnesses who may be in The Hague, not to speak with anyone or communicate in any other way about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given already today or whether that's testimony still to be given tomorrow. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I invite madam usher to escort you out of the courtroom and we will see you back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This leaves us some time for a few procedural matters. I have a few, if we cannot finish them today, we still would have tomorrow. The first one deals with Witness JF-038. On the 12th and the 13th of May of this year, the Chamber has heard the evidence of witness JF-038, and in cross-examination, the Defence put questions to the witness based on a previous statement taken from the witness in 2004. The Simatovic Defence tendered those parts of the statement that were read out before the Chamber in court for admission into evidence, and this can be found at transcript pages 4970 to 4972. The Chamber considers that the tendered parts have been read into the transcript and that this provides sufficient context for the Chamber to understand the witness's answers and assess the witness's evidence and, consequently, denies admission. Mr. Bakrac, I think already I delivered this decision out of an abundance of caution because from those pages of the transcript it appears already that there seem to be no major disagreement and that we started responding to you tendering those documents but when discussing whether the context was sufficient, that you seem not to disagree, although finally you did not withdraw tendering those documents which were never assigned exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. My learned friend Mr. Petrovic spoke to the witness, we have just consulted, and what you are saying is acceptable. And the statement has been recorded in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then what I would now like to do is deliver a decision on the admission of evidence of Husein Ahmetovic pursuant to Rule 92 quater. This is a decision on the Prosecution's motion for admission of evidence of witness Husein Ahmetovic, pursuant to Rule 92 quater which was filed on the 29th of March of 2010. On the 24th of November, 2009, the Prosecution submitted that the witness did not require protective measures at that time. Subsequently, the Prosecution has referred to the witness in public filings. And the Chamber understands that the Prosecution does not intend to seek protective measures for this witness and therefore, refers to him by his name in this decision. On the 29th of March, 2010, the Prosecution filed its motion, in which it sought to admit the evidence of Husein Ahmetovic pursuant to Rule 92 quater of the rules, together with four associated exhibits, the death certificate of the witness, and one additional document. The Prosecution had first tendered the evidence of this witness pursuant to Rule 92 bis of the rules, but due to the new motion, the Chamber now considers moot all outstanding requests pertaining to the application to admit the witness's evidence under Rule 92 bis of the rules. For the sake of expediency, the Chamber will not describe the full procedural history, which is set out in the Prosecution's motion. In a response filed on the 12th of April of this year, the Stanisic Defence requested that the motion be denied, arguing that the criteria for admission pursuant to Rule 92 quater had not been met. On the 16th of April, 2010, the Prosecution requested leave to reply to the Stanisic response. On the 23rd of April, 2010, the Chamber granted leave to reply and informed the parties accordingly through an informal communication. The Prosecution filed its reply on the 28th of April 2010. The Chamber recalls the law governing the admission of evidence pursuant to Rule 92 quater as set out previously by this Chamber in its decision of the 11th of March, 2010 concerning Witness B-179. The Chamber finds that the witness Husein Ahmetovic is deceased and thus unavailable pursuant to Rule 92 quater of the rules. Addressing the Stanisic Defence objection, having reviewed the witness statement, the Chamber notes that it deals in part with acts of the Red Berets for which the accused's responsibility is allegedly incurred. However, it does not deal per se with acts and conduct of the accused as charged in the indictment. When assessing reliability of the witness statement as one of the factors for admission pursuant to Rule 92 quater of the rules, the Chamber considers that the statement was signed by the witness and taken with the assistance of an interpreter duly qualified and approved by the Registry of the Tribunal. Although the statement has not been subject to cross-examination, the statement relates to events about which the Chamber has received other evidence, including the testimony of Witness JF-008 and Witness JF-009. The Stanisic Defence admits that the statement is ambiguous as to the identification of certain persons and therefore lacks clarity. The Chamber considers that the fact that the witness expresses uncertainty with regard to a certain matter, does not by itself render a statement unreliable. The Chamber has considered the ambiguities referred to by the Stanisic Defence and concludes that the witness's statement does not contain any manifest or obvious inconsistencies. In conclusion, the Chamber finds that the witness statement is reliable in the meaning of Rule 92 quater of the rules. The Chamber is further satisfied that the general requirements of admissibility pursuant to Rule 89(C) and (D) have been met. With regards to the associated exhibits tendered by the Prosecution, the Chamber notes that the document with 65 ter number 3609 has already been admitted as P93, and that the document with 65 ter number 3536, has been admitted in relevant part as P94. As for the remaining documents, the Chamber considers that they were discussed by the witness in his statement and form an inseparable and indispensable part of the witness's evidence, and can, therefore, be admitted into evidence. The additional documents, although not discussed by the witness in the proffered statement, may also be admitted into evidence as it is relevant and of probative value and directly relates to and corroborates the witness's evidence. For the foregoing reasons the Chamber grants the motion and admits the following into evidence: The written statement of Husein Ahmetovic of the 11th of July, 2008, which has 65 ter number 5400; the associated exhibits with the 65 ter numbers 118 and 4869; the death certificate for the witness, which has 65 ter number 5273; and the additional document tendered by the Prosecution with 65 ter number 4870. All the mentioned items are admitted publicly. The Registrar is hereby instructed to assign exhibit numbers to the admitted documents and inform the Chamber and the parties of the numbers to be assigned. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. We'll hear later from Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 5400 becomes Exhibit P517. 65 ter 118 becomes Exhibit P518. 65 ter 4869 becomes Exhibit P519. 65 ter 5273 becomes Exhibit P520. And 65 ter 4870 becomes Exhibit P521, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. P517 up to and including P521 are admitted into evidence. I'd like to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The next item is about agreed facts in relation to Witness B-1244. There is a pending Rule 92 quater motion for Witness B-1244 before the Chamber, but there has also been some discussion about whether or not the parties could agree on certain facts related to the witness which could eliminate the need to introduce evidence on the matter. The Prosecution clarified on the 25th of May of this year that there may be room for agreement in relation to very specific matters but that it did not envisage that such agreement would entirely replace the motion for admission into evidence. On the 25th of May, the Chamber invited the parties to come to an agreement, more specifically, invited the Defence to present the Prosecution with a proposal by the 1st of June, and the Prosecution to report on the outcome of the discussion by the 16th of June. The Stanisic Defence has contacted Chamber staff yesterday requesting further time to present its proposal to the Prosecution. The Chamber staff then responded stating that the Chamber agreed, as was also requested by Mr. Jordash, any further submissions on the matter, if there was time and we suspended the initial dead-line on making proposals. Now, Mr. Jordash, most likely there will be -- I think you said you needed 10 to 15 minutes. There's no time for 10 to 15 minutes. There would be time for seven minutes but most likely tomorrow some 10 to 15 minutes would remain. You still think you need the 15 minutes, 10 to 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think so. I'd like to try to persuade Your Honours that we shouldn't do what would you have asked us to do and it wouldn't be a fruitful exercise and I think that would take a little time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that takes more than the seven minutes remaining at this moment we'll delay that until tomorrow because there's a fair expectation that 10 to 15 minutes would remain tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next item on my agenda is about the status of the Stanisic provisional release filings. On the 25th of May, the Prosecution clarified that its request to lift the confidential status of filings in relation to the Stanisic request for provisional release covered four filings. The Stanisic Defence responded that it objected only insofar as the filings revealed detailed information relating to Stanisic's family. On the 27th of May, 2010, the Prosecution informed the Chamber in an e-mailed witness notification that of the four filings, only the response of the 22nd of March, 2010 contained family information, which the Stanisic Defence had asked to remain confidential. Now, what I'm seeking is to have it confirmed on the record that this is the position of the Prosecution and that the Defence agrees with it because if such an agreement exists, then the Chamber, of course, will proceed and later deliver a decision on the matter, but we'd like to be certain that what was suggested that only the 22nd of March filing contained family information is shared by the Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: We can confirm it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the Chamber will deliver the decision in due course. Yes, the last next item is to be dealt with at the end of the examination of the witnesses we heard today. I have no further matters on my agenda. Is there anything the parties would raise in which would take not more than three and a half minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think I have one matter, Your Honour, that we can deal with in that time. And this relates to P164 in evidence. The document was provided to the OTP by SFOR and contains some redactions. On the 19th of February, 2010, the Chamber renewed its invitation to the Prosecution to make inquiries about these redactions and whether SFOR could provide an unredacted copy of the document for the Chamber. On the 10th of May, 2010, the OTP received a reply from SFOR to our inquiry, and I will now report on the matter. The letter we received is from Lawrence Rossin the director of the Balkans task force. Mr. Rossin initiated an inquiry about the document and reported the following: One, that while there is a procedure in place in NATO to track the declassification process, and that such process would record information about such redactions, this particular document was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor's field office in Sarajevo and did not go through that standard. Headquarters controlled redaction/declassification process was not followed, and the consequence of this is that there is no record regarding the declassification for this document. Two, that notwithstanding this, Mr. Rossin, attempted to track the declassification process related to this document, those efforts were unsuccessful. So in the final analysis the Prosecution is unable to provide the Chamber with either an unredacted copy of P164, a document we received with redaction, nor are we able to provide information about the redaction process. And the Prosecution provided the Chamber and Defence teams informally with a copy of this letter last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just for my understanding, if you can't track exactly the declassification process, would there be an original somewhere which is not redacted, which you could look and then look at whether you could provide that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We have no original in our system, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Rossin says that he could not find an original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He cannot find an unredacted original, it's nowhere to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: According to Mr. Rossin he never went through the procedure which would keep track of this, and despite his attempt to investigate the matter, he is unable to provide any additional information about the history of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your report, Mr. Groome. It looks as if we are more or less stuck here. If the Defence would have any further suggestions, we'll hear from them, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think it looks as though the Prosecution have taken it as far as it can be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, we share that opinion, although at this moment we don't know exactly which document this refers to. However, Mr. Groome's explanation is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we leave this matter as it is now and, of course, it is evidence the only problem is that the Chamber was not -- were not very happy with unexplained redactions. If there's nothing else, we'll adjourn, and we'll resume tomorrow -- yes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are not going to add to my bad reputation for interpreters and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Definitely not. I just would ask Your Honours to consider having Dr. Eekhof available tomorrow, if that's possible, if Your Honours are minded to take that course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll consider that, and one of the things we'll also consider whether it would be wise to hear him now or -- because we are talking about most likely about an analysis of what has been found yesterday and today, and the second issue is what to do next week, and how for you to prepare.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider that. Thank you very much. We'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday the 2nd of June, quarter past 2.00, this same Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 2nd day of June, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.
